description: Not independently attested in Cree folklore as a giant whale. The Cree of the plains and subarctic woodlands record no whale spirit; their great water-dwelling monster is the Mishipizhiw or Great Lynx, a dangerous being of deep lakes and rivers who drags people underwater. Where a 'whale giant' is imagined, Cree tradition centers on this underwater lynx and the perils of lakes and rapids.
source: Native-Languages.org, Cree legends and mythology; no Cree whale figure in ethnographic sources
research_notes: No whale giant exists in Cree oral tradition. The Cree water monster is Mishipizhiw (Great Lynx), attested at native-languages.org/cree-legends.htm. The record's culture field is merely 'Canada' with no real tribe, a template artifact. Closest genuine analogue is the underwater lynx, not any whale.

description: Not independently attested as a whale 'guardian' in Maliseet folklore. Whales do appear in Maliseet stories: in 'Turtle Gets a Whale,' Glooscap directs the boastful Turtle to haul a whale ashore for a feast, and the whale's weight presses the overreaching Turtle down until the other animals cut him free. Whales figure as hunted food and wonders of the sea, not protective guardian spirits.
source: Mechling, 'Maliseet Legends,' Journal of American Folklore; native-languages.org Glooskap pages
research_notes: The specific 'whale guardian' being is unattested. Maliseet whale lore centers on Glooscap tales where whales are food/game (e.g., 'Turtle Gets a Whale' in Mechling's Maliseet Legends). The forest-spirit archetype assigned in the record is also wrong for a sea creature.

description: Not independently attested as a whale water-spirit in Maliseet (Wolastoqiyik) tradition. The whale appears as a great sea creature of the coast, a source of food and a test of strength: in 'Turtle Gets a Whale,' Glooscap has the boastful Turtle haul a whale to camp, where its bulk crushes him until the other animals cut it free. Whale tales teach humility, not a whale-spirit guardian.
source: Mechling, 'Maliseet Legends,' Journal of American Folklore vol. 27; Wabanaki Glooscap corpus
research_notes: Duplicate-framed entry with whale-guardian-of-maliseet. The whale is a narrative game animal in Maliseet Glooscap tales, not a water spirit. Whales were coastal food animals for the Maliseet, who lived along the St. John River and the Bay of Fundy.

description: Not independently attested in Shoshone folklore. The Great Basin Shoshone had no coastal or whale traditions, and no whale water-spirit appears in their recorded stories. Their dangerous water beings are the Water Babies, eerie spirits of springs and ponds who lure people to watery deaths, along with lake and river serpents. Whale spirits belong to Arctic, Northwest Coast, and maritime peoples.
source: Native-Languages.org, Paiute/Shoshone legends; Great Basin ethnography
research_notes: Geographically impossible: the Shoshone homeland is the arid Great Basin, far from any ocean. No whale appears in Shoshone oral tradition. Closest Shoshone water beings are the Water Babies and water serpents shared with the Paiute.

description: This record misplaces the being: Iara (or Yara) is the water spirit of Tupi-Guarani lore in Brazil, not of North America. Iara is a beautiful maiden who lives in rivers and sings enchantingly from the water; men who follow her song are drawn beneath the surface and drowned. Some versions describe her with a fish-like lower body. Her homeland is the Amazon and Paraná river basins of South America.
source: Tupi-Guarani tradition; folklore compendia on Iara/Yara
research_notes: Attested as Iara, the Tupi-Guarani river siren of Brazil. The 'USA' attribution is a region error (aliases also list Brazil and Mexico). Consistent with prior batch finding: whitelady-tupi = Iara. Description corrects the geography and identifies the genuine figure.

description: White Painted Woman (Esdzanadehe, also called Changing Woman) is the central culture heroine of Apache tradition. Daughter of the sun, she survived the great flood inside a turquoise mountain and bore the warrior twins Killer of Enemies and Child of the Water, who destroyed the monsters plaguing the world. Apache girls' puberty rites, including the Sunrise Dance, re-enact her power of renewal.
source: folklore.earth, Apache culture page; Western Apache oral tradition
research_notes: Genuine and central Apache figure. Esdzanadehe ('White Painted Woman') is the Apache analogue of Navajo Changing Woman; mother of the Monster Slayer twins; honored in the girls' Sunrise Dance puberty rite. Element/habitat fields in the record are generic but the being itself is fully attested.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ancestor-spirit in Cheyenne tradition. The Cheyenne are a Plains people whose culture heroes and tricksters are other beings: the culture hero Sweet Medicine and the spider trickster Veeho (Wihio). No wildcat or bobcat ancestor figure appears in their recorded mythology; this 'Cheyenne wildcat' record is a misattribution.
source: Native-Languages.org, Cheyenne legends; Grinnell, Cheyenne ethnography
research_notes: Cheyenne trickster is Veeho/Wihio, a spider, not a wildcat (consistent with prior batch B18 finding). Sweet Medicine is the Cheyenne culture hero who organized the Council of 44 and warrior societies. No wildcat ancestor figure exists.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ancestor-spirit in Paiute tradition. Paiute mythology centers on Wolf (Isa), the creator and culture hero, and his younger brother Coyote the trickster; bobcats appear only as minor characters in tales. The wildcat ancestor-spirit is a misattribution. The genuine analogues are Wolf as ancestor-creator and the Water Babies, spirits of springs and ponds.
source: Native-Languages.org, Paiute legends; Wilson Wewa, Legends of the Northern Paiute
research_notes: Paiute creator is Wolf (Isa); Coyote is the trickster brother. A traditional Paiute story 'Bobcat, Cottontail, Coyote' exists, but bobcat is a minor character, not an ancestor-spirit. Water Babies are the real Paiute spirit beings associated with water.

description: The closest attested Cree wildcat being is Mishipizhiw, the Great Lynx or underwater panther, a powerful water monster of Cree and Algonquian tradition who lives in deep lakes and rapids and drags people underwater. It is drawn with catlike features, horns, and a scaly, serpentine body. For the Cree the wildcat of the spirit world is this dangerous water being, not a forest guardian.
source: Native-Languages.org, Cree legends (Mishipizhiw/Great Lynx)
research_notes: Corrected attribution: the genuine Cree wildcat-like being is Mishipizhiw, the Great Lynx/underwater panther. Record's forest-spirit framing is wrong; the being is an aquatic monster. Marked attested with the correction to the real figure.

description: Not independently attested in Inuit tradition. No wildcats or bobcats live in the Arctic, and no wildcat spirit appears in Inuit mythology, whose animal spirits include the polar bear (Nanook), the wolf (Amarok), the raven, and the whale. The record's forest-dwelling wildcat is a misattribution that ignores Inuit geography and oral tradition.
source: Inuit oral tradition; no wildcat figures in Arctic ethnographic sources
research_notes: Anatomically and geographically impossible: there are no felids in the Inuit Arctic. Inuit animal spirits are polar bear (Nanook), wolf (Amarok), raven, whale, etc. The record is a template artifact with a forest habitat field.

description: This entry is wrong on two counts: the Maya are a Mesoamerican people, not of the modern United States, and their feline deity is the jaguar, not a generic 'wildcat.' The Jaguar God of the Underworld, associated with the night sun, caves, and the underworld, is a central Maya deity. This record appears to be a jaguar entry garbled and mislabeled as 'wildcat' and 'USA.'
source: Maya cosmology; Jaguar God of the Underworld references
research_notes: Attested as the Maya jaguar deity (Jaguar God of the Underworld). Region is Mesoamerica, not USA. Consistent with prior batch finding (B14): wildcat-maya maps to the Jaguar God of the Underworld. Description corrects both the species and geography.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat deity in Cherokee tradition. Cherokee animal lore includes the panther as a powerful being, but no deified wildcat figure is recorded; Cherokee spirit animals are more prominently the bear (whose people became the Yonva bear clan) and the wolf. The record likely conflates a generic feline spirit with Cherokee culture, where no such deity appears.
source: Cherokee oral tradition; Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee
research_notes: No Cherokee wildcat deity is attested. Cherokee animal spirits include the bear (Ani-Tsa-gu-hi/Yonva clan origin story) and wolf. Panther appears as a powerful animal but not a deity. Entry is a template misattribution.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat deity in Ute tradition. Ute mythology centers on Sinawav (Coyote) as creator and culture hero, and the wolf plays a major role in Ute origin accounts; no wildcat god or goddess appears in recorded Ute stories. The record is a misattribution, likely generated from a generic feline template rather than Ute oral tradition.
source: Ute oral tradition; native-languages.org Ute pages
research_notes: Ute creator/culture hero is Sinawav (Coyote), consistent with prior batch B18. Wolf figures in Ute creation accounts (wolf carried the heavy bag in one origin myth). No Ute wildcat deity attested.

description: The closest attested Passamaquoddy wildcat being is Lucifee (also Lusifee or Lucivee), a dangerous malevolent wildcat or lynx spirit of Wabanaki lore shared by the Passamaquoddy and Maliseet. Lucifee is a greedy villain who devours animals and people and must be outwitted; he is a monster of appetite, not a ghost. A genuine wildcat spirit exists, but the 'ghost' framing is inaccurate.
source: Native-Languages.org, Lucifee page; Wabanaki oral tradition
research_notes: Attested via Lucifee, the Wabanaki wildcat/lynx spirit (Passamaquoddy and Maliseet). Corrected the 'ghost' framing: Lucifee is a malevolent greedy villain, not a specter. Name etymology uncertain; likely French-Canadian or Lucifer-derived, not Algonquian.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat ghost in Ute tradition. Ute folklore records no ghostly wildcat being; its spirit world includes Coyote-Sinawav, the culture hero, and the wolf of creation accounts. As with other Ute 'wildcat' records, this entry appears fabricated, since no wildcat ghost appears in the ethnographic literature on the Ute.
source: Ute oral tradition; ethnographic collections on Ute mythology
research_notes: No wildcat ghost in Ute tradition. Ute spirit world centers on Sinawav (Coyote) and wolf. Duplicate of the same misattribution pattern seen in wildcat-deity-of-ute. Generated template artifact.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat guardian in Kwakwaka'wakw (Kwakiutl) tradition. The Kwakwaka'wakw of the Northwest Coast have no wildcat guardian figure; their important crests and ancestors include the wolf, raven, killer whale, and bear. In one account the ancestors removed their wolf masks and became human, tying wolf, not wildcat, to origins and chiefly power.
source: Northwest Coast ethnography; Wolf Song of Alaska compilation
research_notes: No wildcat guardian in Kwakwaka'wakw lore. Wolf is the significant animal: a Kwakwaka'wakw myth tells of ancestors removing wolf masks to become human (Steinhart). Northwest Coast crest animals are wolf, raven, killer whale, bear. Misattribution.

description: The Maliseet wildcat figure is Lucifee (Lusifee or Lucivee), a fierce, greedy wildcat-lynx monster of Wabanaki lore, not a benevolent guardian. Lucifee is a dangerous villain who terrorizes the forest and eats smaller animals and unwary people until a clever being outwits him. The 'guardian' framing misrepresents him; he is among the most feared beings in Maliseet and Passamaquoddy stories.
source: Native-Languages.org, Lucifee page; Maliseet/Passamaquoddy tradition
research_notes: Attested via Lucifee, the Maliseet wildcat-lynx monster. Corrected the 'guardian' framing: Lucifee is a malevolent villain, the opposite of a guardian. Duplicate of wildcat-ghost-of-passamaquoddy's underlying figure, a shared Wabanaki being.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat nature-spirit in Apache tradition. Apache mythology is built around figures like White Painted Woman and the warrior twins Killer of Enemies and Child of the Water, with animals such as the mountain lion and coyote appearing in tales; no wildcat or bobcat nature-spirit is recorded. The entry appears to be a generic feline misattribution to the Apache.
source: Apache oral tradition; Legends of America, Apache legends; folklore.earth Apache page
research_notes: No Apache wildcat nature-spirit attested. Apache myth centers on White Painted Woman and the warrior twins. Mountain lion and coyote appear in tales, but not a wildcat spirit. Template misattribution.

description: The Ojibwe wildcat spirit is Bizhiw (Pishiw or Pizhew), the lynx or bobcat of Anishinaabe tradition, also called the Underwater Lynx or Great Lynx. As a totem, Bizhiw is the animal of the Lynx Clan, and in myth the great underwater lynx is a powerful being of lakes and rapids who battles the Thunderbirds and can drag people beneath the water.
source: Great Lakes Now, Ojibwe lynx; native-languages.org; Anishinaabe clan traditions
research_notes: Genuine: Bizhiw is the Ojibwe lynx, a Lynx Clan totem and the Underwater Lynx/Mishipeshu being that fights the Thunderbirds. Region USA applies to Ojibwe communities in Minnesota/Wisconsin/Michigan. Fully attested.

description: The Ojibwe wildcat spirit is Bizhiw, the lynx of Anishinaabe tradition, known across Ojibwe communities in both the United States and Canada. The lynx is the totem of the Lynx Clan and appears as the great underwater lynx, a mighty being of deep lakes who clashes with the Thunderbirds and draws swimmers down. As a nature-spirit it embodies both clan kinship and the dangers of northern waters.
source: Great Lakes Now, Ojibwe lynx; native-languages.org; Anishinaabe clan traditions
research_notes: Canadian twin of wildcatnaturespiritofojibwe-usa. Same genuine being: Bizhiw the lynx, Lynx Clan totem and underwater lynx. Canada flag fits Ontario/Manitoba Ojibwe communities. Fully attested.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat nature-spirit in Pomo tradition. The extensive Pomo folklore recorded by S. A. Barrett centers on the theft of fire, the earth-diver creation, bear shamans, and Coyote; no wildcat or bobcat nature-spirit appears in these collections. The entry is a misattribution, most likely generated from a generic feline template rather than Pomo oral tradition.
source: Barrett, 'Pomo Myths'; Barrett, 'Pomo Bear Doctors'; Pomo traditional narratives
research_notes: No Pomo wildcat spirit attested. Pomo folklore (Barrett 1933, 1917) covers fire theft, earth-diver creation, bear shamans, Coyote cycles. The Pomo are a California Hokan people; no wildcat nature-spirit appears.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat spirit in Cheyenne tradition. Cheyenne mythology knows no wildcat spirit or deity; its sacred figures are the culture hero Sweet Medicine and the trickster Veeho (Wihio) the spider, along with the spirits of the buffalo, wolf, and eagle. This 'Cheyenne wildcat' record is a duplicate misattribution with no basis in recorded Cheyenne folklore.
source: Native-Languages.org, Cheyenne legends; Grinnell, Cheyenne ethnography
research_notes: Duplicate of wildcatancestorspiritcheyenne-usa. Cheyenne trickster is Veeho/Wihio (spider); culture hero is Sweet Medicine. No Cheyenne wildcat spirit exists. Aliases even list Paraguay, Nigeria, and Chile, showing the template artifact.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Cree tradition. The Cree trickster and culture hero is Wisakedjak (Wesakechak), a shapeshifting transformer who rebuilt the world after the flood and whose humorous adventures explain the order of nature; he is not a wildcat. The underwater lynx Mishipizhiw is a Cree wildcat-like being, but it is a dangerous water spirit, never a trickster.
source: Native-Languages.org, Wisakedjak page; Canadian Encyclopedia, Trickster
research_notes: Cree trickster is Wisakedjak/Wesakechak, a transformer, not a wildcat. Mishipizhiw is the Cree wildcat-like water monster but is no trickster. The record conflates the two genuine Cree beings into a false figure.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Haida tradition. The Haida trickster and transformer is Raven (Xhuuya), a shapeshifter who stole the sun, moon, and stars and whose adventures shaped the world. No wildcat or bobcat occupies this role in Haida mythology. The record is a generic trickster misattribution, since Northwest Coast trickster lore belongs to Raven, not to any wildcat.
source: Haida oral tradition; Britannica, Raven cycle; Northwest Coast folklore
research_notes: Haida trickster is Raven (Xhuuya). The Northwest Coast trickster analogue to Coyote is Raven (Britannica). No wildcat trickster exists among the Haida. Template misattribution.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit trickster and culture hero is Raven (Yéil), a shapeshifting transformer whose theft of daylight and other exploits are central to Tlingit oral tradition. Wildcats play no trickster role in Tlingit mythology; the entry is a misattribution, likely generated from a generic template.
source: Tlingit oral tradition; Britannica, Raven cycle; Pacific Northwest folklore
research_notes: Tlingit trickster is Raven (Yéil), consistent with memory of Tlingit lore. No wildcat trickster attested. USA flag fits Southeast Alaska Tlingit. Template misattribution.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat trickster in Tlingit tradition. The Tlingit culture hero and trickster is Raven (Yéil), the transformer who stole the sun and brought light to the world; no wildcat figure plays this role. This Canada-flagged record is a duplicate of the same misattribution, since Tlingit trickster lore centers on Raven across both Alaska and Canada.
source: Tlingit oral tradition; Britannica, Raven cycle; Pacific Northwest folklore
research_notes: Duplicate of wildcattricksteroftlingit-usa. Tlingit trickster is Raven (Yéil). Canada flag fits British Columbia Tlingit (Taku River). No wildcat trickster exists. Template misattribution.

description: Not independently attested as a wildcat water-spirit in Paiute tradition. Paiute water beings are the Water Babies, spirits of springs and ponds who imitate crying infants to lure people into the water, along with great water serpents; no wildcat is associated with water in Paiute lore. The record is a misattribution, possibly confusing the Paiute Wolf creator (Isa) with a feline water being.
source: Native-Languages.org, Paiute legends (Water Babies); Great Basin ethnography
research_notes: No Paiute wildcat water-spirit. The real Paiute water beings are Water Babies. Wolf (Isa) is the Paiute creator but is not aquatic. Misattribution; possibly generated from the same feline template as the other Paiute wildcat entry.

description: Winds figure as living, personified spirits across many Native American traditions. In Navajo belief, Holy Wind (Nilch'i Diyin) is the life-breath that animates all beings; winds guard the four directions at the sacred mountains and appear as spirit people who advise heroes. The Lakota number wind among the aspects of Wakan Tanka, and many Plains peoples revere the four directions.
source: McNeley, Holy Wind in Navajo Philosophy; navajopeople.org Navajo creation; Native Circle four winds
research_notes: Attested concept. Navajo Holy Wind (Nilch'i Diyin) is well documented (McNeley 1981); Wind People appear in the twins' journey in Diné Bahane'. Four directional winds and the Lakota view of wind as an aspect of Wakan Tanka support the general 'wind spirit' figure. The generic 'USA' culture field is broad but the concept is genuine.

description: Not independently attested as a named 'witch bear' in any single Native American tradition, though related themes are widespread. Some tribes tell of bear-women who don a bearskin and become dangerous to their kin, and of bear shamans such as the Pomo Bear Doctors who drew power from bears. The Pawnee Bear Medicine Woman and Cherokee bear-clan stories are the closest genuine analogues.
source: Native-Languages.org, bear legends; Barrett, 'Pomo Bear Doctors'; mythologyblog bear-woman tale
research_notes: No 'witch bear' entity is attested as such. Genuine analogues: bear-woman transformation tales (bearskin cannot be removed, woman kills kin), Pomo Bear Doctors, Pawnee Bear Medicine Woman, Cherokee Yonva bear clan origin. Earlier search for 'Choctaw witch bear' also came up empty, confirming the record is a template.

description: Wohpekumeu is the trickster-transformer and culture hero of the Yurok people of northwestern California, sometimes called 'the Widower.' In Yurok mythology he is a shapeshifter who attempts both beneficial and foolish deeds, helping shape the world and teaching people how to live. His exploits balance comedy with the ordering of the world, and he is among the best-known Yurok figures.
source: Native-Languages.org, Yurok legends; Yurok oral tradition
research_notes: Genuine Yurok figure; slug 'wohpekumen' is a misspelling of Wohpekumeu. He is a trickster/transformer/culture hero of the Yurok of the Klamath River, northern California. Attested.

description: Wolves hold a deep place in Blackfoot tradition as powerful, kinlike beings. In the story of the Wolf Man, a man rescued from murderous wives is adopted by a wolf pack that makes him their brother. The Blackfoot call the Milky Way the Wolf Trail, the road wolves and the dead travel to the sky, and orphaned heroes are befriended by wolves in star legends.
source: Native-Languages.org, Blackfoot legends (The Wolf Man); Blackfoot star lore
research_notes: Attested. The Wolf Man story (man adopted as brother by wolves) is recorded in Blackfoot legend collections (native-languages.org blackfoot-legends.htm). Blackfoot call the Milky Way the Wolf Trail, and the Orphan Boys star legend features wolves befriending abandoned boys. USA flag fits Montana Blackfeet.

description: Wolves are central to Blackfoot (Siksika) tradition on both sides of the Canada-United States border. The Wolf Man story tells of a man saved from his murderous wives and adopted as a brother by wolves, and Blackfoot people call the Milky Way the Wolf Trail, the road wolves follow toward the spirit world. Wolves appear as rescuers and guides in the star legends of the Blackfoot's orphaned heroes.
source: Native-Languages.org, Blackfoot legends (The Wolf Man); Blackfoot star lore
research_notes: Canadian twin of wolfancestorspiritofblackfoot-usa. Same attested figures: Wolf Man, the Wolf Trail (Milky Way), Orphan Boys star legend. Canada flag fits Alberta Siksika/Kainai/Piikani. Genuine.

description: The wolf, nashoba in the Choctaw language, is a respected being in Choctaw tradition. Wolf clans (iksa) exist among the Choctaw, and wolves appear in teaching stories such as 'How the Possum Tricked the Wolves.' The name Neshoba, preserved in Mississippi geography, is the Choctaw word for wolf; he is honored as a relative and clan name-bearer rather than a formal deity.
source: Choctaw Nation cultural materials; 'Shokkata yat Nashoba Alhiha' (Choctaw Cultural Legacy); nashoba = 'wolf'
research_notes: Attested. Nashoba is Choctaw for 'wolf'; Choctaw wolf clans (iksa) exist and wolves appear in teaching stories (Choctaw Cultural Legacy book 'How the Possum Tricked the Wolves'). Record's 'ancestor-spirit' framing overstates: the wolf is a respected clan/totem animal, not a deified ancestor. Southeast burial/village habitat fields are consistent with Choctaw homeland.

description: The wolf is a significant being in Cheyenne tradition, most prominently through the Wolf Warriors, a military society renowned for ferocity and courage in battle that scholars such as George Bird Grinnell linked to the Bowstring Men. Cheyenne medicine men rubbed warrior arrows against wolf fur for success in hunting, and the wolf teaches community and loyalty.
source: Grinnell, Cheyenne ethnography; AAA Native Arts, Cheyenne warrior societies; Wolf Song of Alaska
research_notes: Attested. The Wolf Warriors (Konianutqio) were a Cheyenne military society, possibly identical with the Bowstring Men (Grinnell). Cheyenne medicine men rubbed arrows with wolf fur for hunting success (wolfsongalaska.org). Wolf = community and loyalty in Cheyenne teaching. Not an 'animal-spirit deity' per se but a genuine warrior-society totem.

description: The wolf, ma'iitsoh in Navajo, has two faces in Diné tradition. Gray Wolf is a protector given by Changing Woman to guard the Bitter Water Clan and San Francisco Peaks, and a wolf's howl warns warriors to turn back from a raid. Yet mai-coh, the word for wolf, also means 'witch': skinwalkers are said to wear wolf skins to work evil, so the wolf embodies both protection and misused power.
source: navajopeople.org, Gray Wolf Navajo Protector; Tony Hillerman Portal, 'Navajo wolf'
research_notes: Attested with dual meaning. Gray Wolf (Ma'iitsoh) is a protector of the Bitter Water Clan (Tó dích'íinii) given by Changing Woman (navajopeople.org; San Juan School District curriculum). Simultaneously, 'mai-coh' (wolf) means witch, and skinwalkers are said to don wolf pelts (Tony Hillerman Portal). The record's link to the related entry dily-h-mountain-sheep-people is understandable since both are clan-associated protectors.
